rv.q: But somehow life and joy trickles into this room all the same – the curtains can’t shut everything out. Kristin Scott Thomas plays lady of the house Ranevskaya with a compelling kind of apathy.

Adapted and directed by radical Australian director Benedict Andrews – who staged a similarly disruptive Three Sisters for London’s Young Vic back in 2012 – this lively, irreverent version brings tremendous immediacy to the piece.

Kristin Scott Thomas is back at the Harold Pinter theatre, banishing memories of 2023’s misfiring MeToo comedy drama Lyonesse by tackling, supremely well, Chekhov’s elegiac last masterpiece, The Cherry Orchard.
It's a production that refuses to pin itself down.
But some of the edges are softened, such as the fire of student and would-be revolutionary Trofimov (Jack Riddiford).
This performance is bound to be a night of heartwarming, witty theatre.
Rickson’s direction is masterful, alive to every nuance, confidently embracing the dualities in Chekhov’s text.
Ian Rickson's production doesn't quite catch all the heights and depths of the emotions, the technical efficiency rather limiting the stakes.

All in all, this is a fun and touching restaging of a classic family drama, but the push and pull of this comedic tragedy never quite settles on either mode and cannot always see the wood for the trees.
The result is a confused and incohesive production that feels at odds with the intent of Chekhov’s original.

cn.t: Critics give mixed-to-positive reviews for this Cherry Orchard revival, praising Kristin Scott Thomas's hard-edged, modern Ranevskaya and the haunting production design, though some find the adaptation less memorable than recent stagings.
